description:
Nos presentamos al Hackathon de la NASA para asumir el reto de construir un simulador de misión para astronautas junior. Busco integrantes con habilidades en:

Programación backend / Lógica de juego

Diseño UI/UX e interfaz interactiva

Arte multimedia / Modelado 3D
summary:
Hyper Space is an interactive, educational video game that simulates the challenges of a space mission, allowing players to experience what it takes to manage a base on the Moon or Mars and ensure the survival of its astronauts.

The game offers an experience in which participants must manage essential resources—such as oxygen, energy, food, communications, and radiation protection. Through various scenarios and decision-making moments, players must strike a balance between the mission's requirements, understanding that every choice carries consequences that can determine their ultimate success or failure.

Hyper Space tackles this challenge by transforming complex scientific concepts into a dynamic, accessible, and engaging experience. Furthermore, it draws upon scientific data and information sources from NASA—such as DONKI and OSDR—to ground the learning process in real-world research and advancements in space exploration.

Its significance lies in its ability to foster learning in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), while simultaneously developing critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills. Additionally, it aims to spark interest in space exploration among young people, demonstrating that survival on other worlds requires knowledge, careful planning, and intelligent decision-making.
details:
What does the project do and how does it work? It is an interactive deep-space outpost management simulator (such as lunar or Martian bases) specifically designed for children aged 7 to 12. The player assumes the role of mission commander and must manage critical, constantly competing resources: life support (oxygen and water), radiation shielding, energy budget, food production, and communication delays with Earth. Throughout a mission simulated in turns or daily cycles, every action carries a real opportunity cost (for example, diverting power from the greenhouses to reinforce magnetic shields during a solar storm, or consuming extra oxygen reserves to extend a scientific expedition), allowing the player to immediately see the physical and operational consequences of their decisions.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Experiential engineering learning: Transforms complex concepts of space physics, biology, and resource management into intuitive, playful mechanics that are easy for children to understand.
  • Critical thinking and decision-making: Teaches that in space exploration, no option is free; players develop prioritization, risk management, and problem-solving skills under pressure.
  • Connection to real science: By integrating open NASA datasets (such as space weather alerts from DONKI, biological findings from OSDR, and environmental parameters from Artemis or Mars exploration missions), children interact with authentic scenarios rather than arbitrary rules.

What is the expected impact of the project? To spark scientific and technological (STEM) vocations from an early age, helping young people understand the real engineering and human survival challenges beyond Earth. Beyond offering entertainment, the project aims for every player to finish the game understanding why astronauts and mission planners must constantly balance safety, science, and survival.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used to develop it?

  • Development and code generation: Comprehensive artificial intelligence assistance via ChatGPT to structure the simulator's logic, decision flow, and interactive interface.
  • Core technologies: Web languages and technologies (such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) to ensure accessible, fast execution compatible with any modern browser without complex installations.
  • Data sources: Open datasets and real parameters from NASA (DONKI, OSDR, Artemis missions, and Mars environmental data) adapted to the game's variables.
  • Hardware: Personal computers for programming, playtesting, and fine-tuning the trade-off mechanics.

In what way is the project creative? The creativity lies in translating real aerospace engineering equations and constraints into narrative and visual dilemmas accessible to a 7-to-12-year-old child without losing scientific rigor. Instead of presenting overwhelming data tables, the game turns variables like solar radiation or communication latency into tangible events (such as receiving delayed messages from Earth or seeing changes in the crew's morale and physical condition), allowing learning to happen naturally through experimentation and safe "trial and error."

What factors did the team take into account?

  • Cognitive accessibility and target audience age: Difficulty, vocabulary, and the interface were calibrated so that children aged 7 to 12 can read, understand cause-and-effect relationships, and enjoy the challenge without getting frustrated.
  • Mechanics balance (Trade-offs): A mathematical system was designed where all resources are interconnected, avoiding single "winning" strategies and forcing real strategic decisions in every cycle.
  • Scientific rigor vs. playability: Real NASA data was selected to bring authenticity to mission events, simplifying their timescale so that an entire mission can be played and understood in a dynamic session.
  • Scope and agile prototyping: Priority was given to building a solid, functional playable core by leveraging AI-assisted development tools to clearly demonstrate the resource trade-off mechanic and its educational value.
